li.a: The Sunday Times, Sri Lanka: Slaughter of child monks at Aranthalawa, 35 years on
Ada Derana: AG orders police to launch criminal investigation into 1987 Aranthalawa massacre
Sri Lanka Army, Security Forces Headquarters East: Commemoration of the Aranthalawa Massacre
BBC Sinhala: Vidyananda Maha Pirivena sheltering tsunami victims

content.p: On the morning of 2 June 1987, a red state-run bus carrying young Buddhist monks on a pilgrimage was stopped on a lonely road through teak jungle near Aranthalawa, in Sri Lanka's Ampara District. Within about a quarter of an hour, most of the people on board had been shot or cut down. The Sri Lanka Army and the news site Ada Derana say 33 monks, most of them child novices, and four civilians died, and that the attackers were cadres of the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). The most detailed account, published by the Sunday Times, gives a somewhat different toll. The pages consulted here do not report any trial of the attackers.

The account published by the Sunday Times in 2022, drawn from a research article by Sarita Gunaratna and Dinesh Jayakody, is the most detailed. The authors say it rests on interviews with survivors, eyewitnesses, first responders and relatives, and on sworn statements and affidavits gathered by the armed forces and police.

On the night of 1 June the head monk, Venerable Hegoda Sri Indasara Nayaka Thero, went to the Sri Vidyananda Pirivena, a monastic school, where the child monks were waiting, excited about the next day's trip. They travelled together to the Mahawapi temple. The monks rose at 4 a.m. for their morning observances. Shortly after 5 a.m. a red Sri Lanka Transport Board bus bearing a "Special Tour" placard arrived. Its driver, G. G. Samarapala, was a supporter of the temple.

Each boy carried a talipot leaf fan and a cloth bag holding a spare robe, an alms bowl, a needle and thread and a parcel of lunch. A white van carried the monks who did not fit on the bus. At 5:45 a.m. the bus left with 43 monks, 39 of them children, and four lay people, according to the Sunday Times. The boys sang folk songs until the head monk mock-scolded them and told them to chant pirith, the protective Buddhist verses, instead. The bus crossed from Ampara District into Batticaloa District on the road towards Kandy.

AmazingLanka, a Sri Lankan heritage site, describes the journey as a pilgrimage from Mahavapi Vihara to the Kelaniya Raja Maha Vihara, both sacred Buddhist sites. Its figures differ from the Sunday Times: it speaks of 33 novice monks aboard. It also gives the time of the halt as 7:15 a.m.

The route was watched. Special Task Force (STF) officers stationed at the Mangalagama camp had been patrolling the road since the night before, protecting what the Sunday Times calls the last Sinhalese village in Batticaloa. They saw the bus pass, followed a little later by the van. Around 7 a.m., A. W. Jayawardene, the chief home guard of the hamlet of Nuwaragaltenna, was drinking tea at his roadside house after a night shift. He caught sight of the bus and heard the monks chanting inside.

At about 7:15 a.m. the bus reached a desolate stretch of the road through the Aranthalawa jungle. A log lay across the road. The conductor, Jinadasa, suggested driving over it, but Samarapala began to reverse. Three men in navy-blue uniforms resembling those of the Air Force appeared. One, holding an assault rifle, signalled the bus to stop. Samarapala complied, believing the man was a member of the security forces who needed a lift.

The man boarded with two others and, speaking in Tamil, ordered Samarapala to turn into the jungle. Samarapala, who the account says was fluent in Tamil, told him he was a civilian with six children of his own and that his passengers were child monks on a pilgrimage. The gunman pointed his weapon at the driver's mouth and repeated the order. Samarapala obeyed. According to the account, those on board saw 25 to 30 cadres armed with guns, swords, machetes, knives and poles moving silently on foot beside and behind the bus. The children began to cry.

About 50 metres in, the cadre in charge told the driver to cut the engine. The account says another, who looked about 17, went through the bus taking watches and wallets from the lay passengers; the monks handed over what little money they had. The first cadre then returned and shot Samarapala several times in the head, as he begged for his children's sake.

A cadre carrying a sword climbed aboard. The Sunday Times reports that Venerable Hegoda Sri Indasara, 59, stood and said he was not afraid to die: "If you harbor hatred towards me, then kill me! But, do not harm these little ones." He was pushed back into his seat and struck. The sword first hit the ceiling, he raised an arm to block it, and the blade struck his head. He died in his seat.

Venerable Valallawita Wimalanyana Thero, seated directly behind, stood up and deflected the next blow with his arm. The deflected blade sliced his hand, arm and chest, and he fell between the seats and survived. From the floor he watched blood run down the aisle. The children begged for their lives. The account records the Sinhala words "Aney mame, epa" ("Uncle, don't") and a plea to the attackers as "big brother" not to kill them.

The attackers then left. Wimalanyana heard whoops and laughter and shots fired into the air. The account says the whole attack lasted ten to fifteen minutes, and that survivors later described the attackers as practised and efficient.

Jayawardene had heard gunfire not long after the bus passed. He sounded a siren, gathered his home guards within minutes and asked a lorry driver whether he had seen the monks' bus. He had not. Jayawardene sent two men to the nearest STF camp and led the remaining 23, armed with rifles, axes and poles, into the jungle.

The white van's driver had stopped some way behind the bus. The account says the men who stopped the bus fired on the van, which was not hit. He turned around and raced back to the STF patrol, around 45 minutes after the vehicles had passed them. He told SI Janaka Hapuhinna he had seen about eight men near the bus. With no vehicle of their own, the officers flagged down lorries, climbed aboard and followed the gunfire into the trees. About 50 metres from the diversion they found the bus with its windows blown out, "eerily quiet".
The figures differ between sources.

The Ada Derana news site and the Sri Lanka Army both say the LTTE killed 33 monks, most of them child novices, and four civilians. Ada Derana adds that three monks escaped with critical injuries. The Sunday Times account itself gives a different count: of 47 people who boarded the bus that morning, 34 were killed; 31 of the dead were monks, 29 of them child monks, and of the four lay volunteers, three were killed. AmazingLanka says 31 novice monks and four laypersons died and that four monks survived, one permanently disabled. The BBC Sinhala report of 2005 also refers to thirty-one bodies of slain monks. The pages do not reconcile these totals.

According to the Sunday Times, the STF learned of the team chiefly by monitoring LTTE radio traffic. The name that stood out was an eastern regional leader known as Regan, whom the STF named as having led the operation and taken the main part in it. He belonged to a group of eight LTTE leaders based in Batticaloa. The STF also believed that Karuna Amman, the LTTE commander in the east, would have known of the attack. These are the STF's identifications, reported in that account.

It says that a week later a five-man STF team led by SI Faizal Hadji ambushed a camp in the Unnichchai forest and killed three of the eight leaders; two more were killed in a later operation. Regan survived. The LTTE leadership, the account says, took pains to keep him alive, sending him to South India for treatment after he was injured. He later received political asylum in France, lived in Paris under the name Nadarajah Matheenthiran and was granted French citizenship. By 2002 he was said to lead the LTTE's front organisation in France, the Tamil Coordinating Committee. On 8 November 2012 he was shot dead near a bus stand in Paris by two assailants on a motorcycle. The account says French authorities believe members of a rival LTTE faction killed him.

The government offered one-time compensation of Rs. 25,000 for each adult killed and Rs. 15,000 for each child. The Sunday Times calls this a paltry sum even by 1987 standards. Some families, including the head monk's, rejected it; most families were too poor to refuse. The victims' families received no further assistance, and the survivors received nothing.

The mother of Venerable Wavinne Aththadassi Thero, who died at 17, D. M. Siriyawathi, said her family's entire payment was consumed obtaining her son's death certificate, after which they sank deeper into poverty. She continued visiting the pirivena, where the monks gave her tea, sugar and medicine. She died in 2022, less than two weeks after being diagnosed with liver cancer in May, as hospitals across the island ran out of medicine.

AmazingLanka says the Helabima Organisation and the STF built a monument near the site in 2003, and that in 2013 a memorial museum was created using the same bus, with the final minutes re-created inside it. A newer monument with a statue of the head monk stands by the road.

The Vidyananda Maha Pirivena itself took on a different role in 2005. BBC Sinhala reported after the tsunami that the hall where thirty-one slain monks' bodies had lain was sheltering around a thousand displaced people, most of them Tamil. The head monk, Venerable Kirindiwela Somarathana, said the temple had made itself a sanctuary for them.

In June 2020 Venerable Andaulpatha Buddhasara Thero, who was critically injured in the attack, filed a fundamental rights petition in the Supreme Court seeking prosecution of living former LTTE members who took part. In October 2020 Attorney General Dappula de Livera directed the acting IGP to record the victim's statement and begin a criminal investigation, with a progress report due in two weeks. The pages consulted do not say how the case ended.

On 2 June 2025, the 38th anniversary, a commemoration was held at the Aranthalawa International Buddhist Centre. The Sri Lanka Army says Major General P. R. Pathiravithana, commander of Security Forces East, attended, and a foundation stone was laid for a new building near the monument.
